p.chapo: Since 1978, the same line has linked Saint-Malo and Pointe-à-Pitre. 3,542 nautical miles of English Channel, Bay of Biscay, trade winds and squalls, sailed single-handed.
p.obsIntro: The course is full of hazards and risk areas: CPZs (cetacean protection zones), TSSs (traffic separation schemes), mats of sargassum, drifting logs and containers adrift. These dangers, sometimes invisible, demand constant vigilance from the skippers.

obstacles.alt: A mat of sargassum seen from the air
obstacles.x: These brown algae float on the surface and drift in rafts across the tropical Atlantic, sometimes for miles. Approaching the West Indies, they wrap around rudders, daggerboards and foils and slow the boat down. The skipper has to ease off, sometimes back up or even dive to clear them, losing precious seconds every time.

obstacles.alt: A cargo ship on the horizon at dusk
obstacles.x: Traffic Separation Schemes are the motorways of commercial shipping, notably off Ushant and Cape Finisterre. They are closed to sailing boats and the skippers must go around them. But even outside these zones, the skippers must watch out for these giants, day and night, from the very first hours of the race.

obstacles.alt: Two containers adrift in the swell
obstacles.x: Logs, drifting containers, fishing nets: these unidentified floating objects are invisible at full speed and can break a rudder, a foil or a hull.

obstacles.alt: Two whales seen from the air
obstacles.x: Whales, sperm whales, rorquals and dolphins cross the skippers' path: the ocean is their natural habitat. To protect these animals and the skippers, cetacean protection zones are defined along the course. These zones are off-limits to the skippers, who must go around them to avoid any collision.

p.meteoIntro: 3,542 nautical miles between Saint-Malo and Pointe-à-Pitre in November: the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe offers a wide variety of weather situations, explained in three parts by Cyrille Duchesne, the race's weather expert for Météo Consult, partner of the solo transatlantic race.

bulletins.t: Between a disturbed westerly flow and the Azores high
bulletins.ou: English Channel and Bay of Biscay
p: In November, the atmospheric circulation is generally disturbed in the English Channel and then in the Bay of Biscay, under the influence of the oceanic westerly regime.

The Azores high usually sits further south than in summer, so it no longer builds a ridge (an extension) towards the Bay of Biscay; on the contrary, it tends to retreat towards the Azores. So in 70 to 80% of cases, there is a westerly to south-westerly regime, with low-pressure systems moving across the North Atlantic. This often brings an alternation of south-south-westerly winds ahead of the fronts and west-north-westerly winds behind the cold fronts, with more or less strong conditions as the cold front goes through: if the lows track over the British Isles, the fleet is on the edge of these systems, which brings fairly strong winds. If, on the other hand, the lows stay further north towards Iceland, the fronts are weaker and the winds less sustained.

Two other scenarios, less frequent at this time of year, are possible. The fleet can find itself on the edge of a high sitting between the British Isles and the North Sea, which brings a north-easterly wind: more favourable conditions for the start, allowing the boats to get out of the Channel and clear the Bay of Biscay fairly quickly. The other scenario, even less frequent, is an Azores high positioned further north, as in summer, with lighter conditions and a ridge that cuts off the southern route in the Bay of Biscay, forcing the sailors to go around it to the north.

Whatever the configuration, the opening phase of the Route du Rhum - Destination Guadeloupe is often decisive: the sailors must constantly strike a balance between sailing fast to be the first to catch the trade winds and managing a weather situation that can be very unsettled, and therefore likely to cause damage if they end up in very strong conditions.

bulletins.t: The trade-wind route, not always so peaceful
p: Once out of the Bay of Biscay, past Cape Finisterre, the key question is at what latitude the trade winds can be picked up. It all depends on the position of the famous Azores high: if it is in its average position for the time of year, right over the Azores, the trade winds are usually found fairly quickly, from Madeira, or between Madeira and the Canaries. If the high sits further south, the trade winds will be very far south, between the Canaries and Cape Verde.

From there, three options open up. The first is to pass north of the Azores high. The advantages: it is the most direct route and the boats benefit from the Atlantic fronts, which means sustained wind. The drawbacks: it is mostly upwind sailing, so harder conditions, and there is a risk of finding lighter winds on the way down to the trade winds.

The second option, the opposite of the first, is to head south to look for the trade winds. The risk is making the route considerably longer, especially by diving very far south; the advantage is that once in the trade winds, the boats benefit from a stronger regime, known as the deep trades, which carries them across the Atlantic at great speed.

The third option is a middle course, with a southerly route at first but a shorter detour and moderate trade winds. It is a trade-off between distance and speed, and the choice is often made quite early, off Portugal.

People sometimes think of the trade wind as a constant wind, fairly steady for the whole Atlantic crossing: far from it. The trade wind can vary enormously in strength and direction. While the average winds are around 15 to 20 knots from the north-east, they can rise to 35 to 40 knots when the air is unstable or, on the contrary, drop into what are called “trade-wind failures”, with lower pressure and small transition zones with no wind, especially between the Azores high and the Bermuda high. The sailors have to go along with the trade wind's moods.

The state of the sea also plays a part: when there are deep lows over the Atlantic, they can create cross seas, with on one side a north-westerly swell from these lows, which travels quite far south, and on the other a sea built up by the north-easterly trade wind. It is fairly uncomfortable.

Approaching the West Indies, there is generally more instability, because the boats are further from the high and closer to the Intertropical Convergence Zone (the Doldrums), a vast low-pressure area with less wind and more instability. This brings areas of squalls, either isolated or in more organised lines known as easterly waves, with big variations in the wind as the boats go through them. It calls for vigilance from the sailors, with many manoeuvres and sail adjustments.

Isolated squalls also have to be negotiated carefully, sometimes with a sudden increase in wind as the squall approaches and, behind it, calm patches where a boat can come to a standstill. The sailor's experience and observation help them get through these storm clouds, which can be spotted from a distance.

Along the arc of the Lesser Antilles, the sailors have to handle the wind shadows of the islands as well as possible or, on the contrary, the stronger winds between two islands: they need to know exactly where to go so as not to get caught out. And finally, the lap around Guadeloupe is often laborious, in the wind shadow of La Soufrière, usually with a good deal of nervous and physical tension.
